where: Section 2 (also Exam traps item 1 and Quiz Q5 answer)
problem: The chapter says tie lines 'come out horizontal only on a right-angled plot with A on the vertical axis'. They do not. On a right-triangular plot with A as ordinate and S as abscissa, the two equilibrium layers generally have different A contents, so the tie line joining them slopes. What is horizontal on such a plot is a line of constant A content, which is not a tie line. Teaching the reverse rule makes a student accept a wrong extract composition on a right-angled diagram.
fix: Tie lines slope on the equilateral triangle, and they slope on a right-angled ternary plot as well. On both plots the horizontal lines are lines of constant A, not tie lines. Only the distribution plot (y against x) collapses each tie line to a single point.

where: Section 2, end of the systems classification
problem: Type 2 is described as 'the two-phase band hugs one corner', implying a single band. Two partly miscible pairs give two separate two-phase regions, one along each of the two sides that meet at the shared corner. The type 3 sentence ('a two-phase band crosses the diagram') is also loose.
fix: Type 2: two pairs are partly miscible, so two separate two-phase regions run along two sides and come together near the corner shared by the two partly miscible pairs. Type 3: all three pairs are partly miscible, giving three two-phase regions, one along each side, and where three liquids coexist a small three-phase region in the middle.

problem: The second sentence, 'A second layer would have to have a composition on the curve, which is not available at that overall composition', is vague: 'not available' does not say what fails. A student may read it as a matter of solubility rather than of the mass-balance lever rule on a tie line.
fix: Outside the curve the mixture is one stable liquid phase. To split into two layers, the overall composition must sit on a straight line joining two points of the binodal curve, that is on a tie line. No tie line passes through a point outside the curve, so one phase is the only possible state.
